questions.prompt: Which of these words belongs to the LEISURE field?
questions.explanation: "instrument" belongs to the LEISURE field: the lesson groups it with play, games, reading and music, the words for what you do in your free time. "carrots" is a FOOD word, "grandfather" is a FAMILY word, and "elephant" is an ANIMALS word.

questions.prompt: Which adjective of the lesson describes a person who is boring and has nothing lively to say?
questions.explanation: "dull" is the adjective for somebody boring, with nothing lively to say. "bright" is its opposite and describes somebody clever, quick to understand; "kind" describes somebody who thinks of other people and helps them; and "sociable" describes somebody who enjoys being with other people.

questions.prompt: Complete: "On feast days all our ___ come to our house: my uncles, my aunts and their children."
questions.explanation: "relatives" is the word here: it covers the whole wide family, uncles and aunts and cousins and grandparents together. "parents" is the trap a French speaker walks into, because in English it means your mother and your father and nobody else. "cousins" names only the children of your uncles and aunts, and "grandparents" names your father's and your mother's parents, not the uncles and the aunts of this sentence.

questions.prompt: "Is your sister kind?" Which answer makes the two moves of the lesson, yes or no and then the fact?

options.text: Yes, she is kind, and everybody in our family says so.
Yes, she is kind: she carries our neighbour's bags upstairs.
Yes, she is kind: she is a very nice and friendly girl.
Yes, she is very kind, and I am kind to my little sister too.

questions.explanation: "Yes, she is kind: she carries our neighbour's bags upstairs." makes the two moves: yes, then one fact that proves the adjective. "Yes, she is kind: she is a very nice and friendly girl." only piles up more adjectives, and a second adjective never proves the first one. "Yes, she is kind, and everybody in our family says so." reports an opinion instead of a fact, and "Yes, she is very kind, and I am kind to my little sister too." talks about you rather than about her.

questions.prompt: Your cousin reads every evening, and you read every evening too. Which sentence compares you the way the lesson does?

options.text: We are like: we both read every evening.
We are alike: we both read every evening.
I am like to her: we both read every evening.
We like each other: we both read every evening.

questions.explanation: "We are alike: we both read every evening." is right: alike stands on its own and says that two people are similar. "We are like: we both read every evening." leaves like without the person you are compared to, and like always needs one, as in I am like her. "I am like to her: we both read every evening." adds a preposition that English never uses after like. "We like each other: we both read every evening." says you enjoy each other's company, which is a different idea altogether.
